Lesson

The Depression at Home

Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

How did ordinary Americans live when the money ran out, and what did they begin to ask of their government?

The Depression was a catastrophe for millions, but not the same catastrophe for everyone. This lesson follows families into Hoovervilles, onto the Great Plains, and to Washington with the Bonus Army, and ends with the election of 1932.

Objectives
  1. I will be able to describe how the Great Depression changed daily life for families in cities and on farms
  2. I will be able to explain why some groups, including Black Americans and Mexican Americans, suffered more than others
  3. I will be able to analyze the Bonus Army episode as a test of the relationship between citizens, the president, and the Army
Quick Check-in

If your neighbors lost their jobs and had nothing to eat, who should help them first? (No wrong answer. Just check in with yourself.)

The Book
Parts 1 to 3
?
⚡ DECIDE FIRST
Picture two families in 1932. In one, a parent still has a job. In the other, a parent has lost one.
Why would the Depression feel so different in each home? Decide first and jot down two reasons before you open this.
For the family with a job, falling prices made the paycheck go further. For the family that lost one, the income stopped at once, because there was no unemployment insurance and no federal system of help. They might lose savings to a bank run or their home to foreclosure. The lesson says the Great Depression was a catastrophe for millions, but not the same catastrophe for everyone.
⚡ TRY IT · WHO WAS HIT HARDEST?
The hard times did not fall evenly. Check what you remember about who suffered most.
1. In some northern cities, how did Black unemployment compare with white unemployment?
2. In Los Angeles in 1931, officials chartered trains to carry Mexican American families to Mexico. Why did they favor this?
⚡ HOW WELL DID IT HOLD UP?
Hoover counted on voluntary help from families, churches, and charities. How well did that hold up as hard times went on?
⚡ PUT IT IN ORDER
Put the events of the summer of 1932 in order. Tap them one at a time.
    Verdict

    Who Should Help When the Money Runs Out?

    My Verdict

    1.Was the voluntary help of neighbors, churches, and local charities enough, or did the disaster call for the national government? Decide, then defend your verdict with one fact from the book that supports you and one fact that cuts against you.

    The chapter on relief says what neighbors and churches did, and why cities and private charity ran dry. It ends by asking whether the national government should provide relief.

    My Notebook
    Keep This in Mind

    The Depression was not the same catastrophe for everyone. When voluntary help ran dry, Americans began to ask what the national government owed its citizens.

    Ask Mr. Magister

    The Crash and the Depression

    The Depression at Home

    Part 1

    When the Jobs Disappeared

    Chapter 1Jobless and Losing Homes
    Chapter 2Hoovervilles and Breadlines
    Chapter 1

    Jobless and Losing Homes

    By 1932, about one American worker in four had no job. Economists measure this with the unemployment rate, the share of people who want to work but cannot find a job. The country had no unemployment insurance and no federal system of relief. Wisconsin passed the first state law for unemployment insurance that same year, but it did not pay anything right away. A worker who lost a job often lost the family's income at once. Savings had often disappeared in the bank runs you read about last time. Families fell behind on their mortgage payments, and banks took their homes in a foreclosure. Farm families lost their land the same way. In 1932 and 1933, farmers in several states crowded into the sales of foreclosed farms and scared off other bidders. Neighbors would bid a few pennies, and the farm would be sold back to the family for almost nothing.

    Daily life changed in many small ways. Families doubled up, with grandparents, cousins, and grown children crowding under one roof. Couples put off marriage, and the birth rate fell. Schools suffered too. Some districts shortened the school year, and some rural schools closed early, because the money had run out. Many teenagers left school to work or left home to ride freight trains in search of jobs, and there were hundreds of thousands of them. Some families sent a son away because it meant one less mouth to feed. The young riders slept in railyards and begged for food at back doors, and the trains were dangerous. Many wives took in laundry or sewing to bring in a little money, and more married women looked for jobs. A law passed in 1932 said that if both a husband and a wife worked for the federal government, one of them had to resign, and most of the people who lost their jobs were women.

    Chapter 2

    Hoovervilles and Breadlines

    Those who lost their homes built shacks out of crates and scrap metal on the edges of cities. These shantytowns were bitterly named Hoovervilles, after the president. The one in Seattle lasted for nine years. Men turned their empty pockets inside out and called them Hoover flags. A car pulled by a horse or mule, because its owner could no longer afford gasoline, was called a Hoover cart, and the stew ladled out at soup kitchens was sometimes called Hoover stew. Men who slept outdoors pulled newspapers over themselves for warmth and called them Hoover blankets. In the cities, hungry people stood in a breadline outside churches and charities waiting for free food. On city streets, men in once-good suits sold apples for five cents apiece to earn a few coins. Many felt deep shame. They had always worked hard, and now they could not feed their families.

    It is also true that three out of four workers still had jobs, even in the worst year. For those who kept working, falling prices made the paycheck go further. Prices fell by nearly a quarter between 1929 and 1933. The Great Depression was a catastrophe for millions, but it was not the same catastrophe for everyone.

    Part 2

    Hardest Hit

    Chapter 3Spirits, Strains, and Unequal Burdens
    Chapter 4The Dust Bowl
    Chapter 5When the Money Ran Out
    Chapter 3

    Spirits, Strains, and Unequal Burdens

    People also found ways to lift their spirits. Movie theaters stayed busy, because a dime bought a few hours of escape. Some gave away a dish with every ticket to bring in customers on slow nights. Families gathered around the radio for comedy, music, and baseball. In 1935, a board game called Monopoly, in which players buy property and grow rich, became a surprise hit. Historians often note the irony of a nation of poor families playing at wealth. It suggests that Americans held on to hope even when their daily lives gave them little reason.

    Some groups were hit much harder. Black Americans were often "last hired, first fired." In some northern cities, Black unemployment ran twice as high as white unemployment, or worse. In the South, Black sharecroppers and farm workers had been poor before the crash, and now they had almost nothing. Local relief offices often helped white families first. In some places, Black families were given smaller amounts than white families, or were turned away. Justice could be harsh as well. In 1931, nine Black teenagers riding a freight train through Alabama were accused of attacking two white women. Within weeks, an all-white jury had sentenced eight of them to death. The case, known by the name of the town of Scottsboro, drew attention across the country and around the world, and the Supreme Court later ordered new trials because the young men had not had proper lawyers.

    Mexican Americans in the Southwest and elsewhere faced a different pressure. Officials in many cities and counties pushed families to leave the country, a policy called repatriation. Hundreds of thousands of people went to Mexico, some under pressure and some by force, and many of them were American citizens who had been born in the United States. In Los Angeles in 1931, agents raided a public plaza where Mexican families gathered. Local officials found that chartering a train to Mexico cost less than keeping a family on relief, and trains left carrying hundreds of people at a time.

    Chapter 4

    The Dust Bowl

    On the Great Plains, nature added a second disaster. Farm prices had been falling since the 1920s. Then, beginning in 1931, a severe drought struck. In earlier years, farmers had plowed up the tough prairie grass to plant wheat, encouraged by high wartime prices and by the new tractor, which let a family farm far more land than horses could. Now nothing held the soil in place. Winds lifted the dry dirt into huge clouds, some of them miles high, that turned noon into night. One of the worst, on April 14, 1935, was remembered as Black Sunday. The region came to be called the Dust Bowl. Crops died, animals choked, and families gave up. Hundreds of thousands left the Plains, and many headed west to California in old trucks piled high with their belongings. Many followed U.S. Route 66, the highway that ran from Chicago across the Plains to Los Angeles. Most came from Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas, and Missouri, but Californians called them all "Okies," a name that was often meant as an insult. In April 1935, a soil expert named Hugh Bennett was testifying to a committee of Congress about the danger when dust from the Plains reached Washington and dimmed the sky. He is said to have pointed toward the window and told the senators that this was what he had been talking about. Congress soon passed a soil conservation law.

    Chapter 5

    When the Money Ran Out

    What did Americans do when the money ran out? The republican tradition says that a healthy civic culture produces cooperation without orders from above, and this happened across the country. Neighbors shared food. Churches ran soup kitchens. Lodges, unions, and local charities collected money. People traded work for meals. Some towns printed their own paper money, called scrip, to keep local trade going. President Hoover had counted on exactly this kind of voluntary help, and for a time it worked. But the scale of the disaster was too great. Cities depended on property taxes, and when homeowners could not pay, the cities lost the money they needed to help the poor. Cities went broke, and some could not pay their teachers. In Chicago, teachers went months without pay. Private charity ran dry. In 1931, New York's governor, Franklin D. Roosevelt, set up a state relief program with state money, run by a social worker named Harry Hopkins, who would soon matter much more, and some other states followed. Relief, in this sense, means money or goods given directly to people in need. Local relief usually came with strings. An investigator visited the home to ask what the family owned and who in it could work, and help often arrived as an order for groceries instead of cash. A family had to show that it had almost nothing left before it received anything. The question was whether the national government should provide it.

    Part 3

    The Bonus Army

    Chapter 6Veterans March on Washington
    Chapter 7The Army Clears the Camp
    Chapter 8Roosevelt Wins
    Chapter 6

    Veterans March on Washington

    Anger was rising even before that summer. In March 1932, thousands of jobless workers marched to the Ford plant in Dearborn, Michigan, to ask for work. Guards and police fired on the crowd, and at least four marchers were killed. The sharpest test came in the summer of 1932. In 1924, Congress had promised veterans of the Great War a bonus, but not to be paid until 1945. In 1932, that meant waiting thirteen more years. The promise took the form of a certificate worth about a dollar for each day served at home and a dollar and a quarter for each day overseas. With no jobs, many veterans wanted the money right away. In the spring and summer, thousands of them marched to Washington. The march began in Portland, Oregon, in May, led by a former sergeant named Walter Waters, and men joined along the way, hopping freight trains and hitching rides. Together with their families, perhaps twenty thousand or more camped in shacks and tents, many of them across the Anacostia River from the Capitol. They called themselves the Bonus Army. Washington's police chief, Pelham Glassford, himself a former general, treated them kindly and helped find food and tents. The camp had streets and rules and a daily routine, and the men organized themselves by state.

    The House passed a bill to pay the bonus early, but the Senate voted it down on June 17. Thousands of veterans waited on the Capitol grounds for the news. When they heard, they did not riot. They sang "America" and walked back to their camps. Many veterans then went home, but thousands stayed.

    Chapter 7

    The Army Clears the Camp

    On July 28, police tried to clear some buildings that the veterans occupied. Shots were fired, and two veterans were killed. Hoover then ordered the Army to clear the area. General Douglas MacArthur led the troops, which included infantry, cavalry with drawn sabers, and tanks. Major George Patton led the cavalry, and MacArthur's aide, Major Dwight Eisenhower, thought the Army's chief of staff should not be there at all. They used tear gas and drove the veterans across the river. MacArthur went farther than the president had ordered. He crossed the bridge and cleared the main camp, which went up in flames, even though Hoover had told the troops to stay on the near side. MacArthur told reporters that the marchers were a mob close to revolution. Americans watched the scene in newsreels. Hoover claimed that many of the veterans were Communists and criminals, but investigators found that most were genuine veterans. The country was shocked at the sight of soldiers turning on men who had once worn the same uniform.

    Chapter 8

    Roosevelt Wins

    Whatever Hoover intended, the damage was done. It raised a hard question about the Republic. Who commands the Army, and how far may it go in dealing with citizens who are protesting? The bonus itself was not forgotten. In 1936, Congress passed a bill to pay it early, and it did so over President Roosevelt's veto. You will read Hoover's own explanation of these events in the next page.

    That November, voters gave their answer to the larger question. Roosevelt, the Democratic governor of New York, defeated Hoover in a landslide. In July, he had broken with custom by flying to the party's convention in Chicago to accept the nomination in person, instead of waiting at home to be told. He carried forty-two of the forty-eight states, and he won 472 electoral votes to Hoover's 59. But the new president would not take office until March 1933. In the long wait, the banks kept failing and the country sank deeper. Hoover asked Roosevelt to join him in a common plan, but Roosevelt did not want to be tied to Hoover's policies, and he refused. The 20th Amendment, ratified in January 1933, would shorten that wait for future presidents, but it did not apply to this one. The story of what Roosevelt did when he arrived is the subject of the next week.
